title: Text Formatter: how it works, formula and examples
excerpt: Text Formatter: Change text case — UPPERCASE, lowercase, Title Case and Sentence case. Learn how to use it, the formula behind it, a worked example and…
content:
The [Text Formatter](/text-formatter) is a free online tool on CalcHub. Change text case — UPPERCASE, lowercase, Title Case and Sentence case. Enter your text to format and format and the result appears straight away — no account or download needed. Because it runs entirely in your browser, the values you type never leave your device, and you can use it as often as you like.

Change the capitalisation of any text in one click: UPPERCASE, lowercase, Title Case, Sentence case, or Capitalise Each Word. Paste in a heading, a title, a paragraph or a whole document and get the reformatted version instantly — no retyping, no find-and-replace. Title Case follows the usual style-guide rule of leaving small words (a, an, the, and, of, in) lowercase unless they start or end the title. This guide explains how to use it, the formula it applies, and a worked example you can follow with your own numbers.

## How to use the Text Formatter

Start by typing or pasting your text to format, then choosing your format from the list. The result updates as you type, so adjust any value and watch the answer change. If the answer is not what you expected, check the value you entered first — a missing digit or a wrong unit is the usual cause.

1. Paste or type the text you want to reformat.
2. Choose the case: UPPERCASE, lowercase, Title Case, Sentence case or Capitalise Each Word.
3. Copy the formatted text from the result — the word and character counts are shown below it.

## How it works

The [Text Formatter](/text-formatter) works straight from the values you enter: change an input and the result updates immediately, with no page reload and no waiting. Everything happens in your browser, so your entries never leave your device. Try it with a few different values and you will quickly get a feel for how the inputs move the result.

## Worked example

Here is a typical example. “the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog” in Title Case becomes “The Quick Brown Fox Jumps Over the Lazy Dog”. The same sentence in UPPERCASE is “THE QUICK BROWN FOX JUMPS OVER THE LAZY DOG”. Try the same figures in the [Text Formatter](/text-formatter) and you will get the same result — then change one value at a time to see how the answer moves.

## What the result shows

With the default values (Text to format: the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog. it was a bright cold day in april., Format: Title Case), the [Text Formatter](/text-formatter) returns Formatted text: The Quick Brown Fox Jumps Over the Lazy Dog. It Was a Bright Cold Day in April., Words: 17, Characters: 79. The first figure is the headline result, and the rest break it down so you can see how the total is made up. If you want to compare with a related calculation, the [Word Counter](/word-counter) is worth a look before you finish.

## When to use each case

UPPERCASE is for warnings, labels and emphasis — never for long passages, because it is harder to read. Title Case is the standard for headings, book titles and article titles. Sentence case (first word capitalised, the rest lowercase) is the norm for body text and for most website headings today. Lowercase is mostly for code, file names and identifiers, where capitals can break things.

## How Title Case handles small words

Style guides disagree on the details, but the common rule is: capitalise every word except a, an, the, and, but, or, of, in, on, to, for and similar short words — unless one of them is the first or last word of the title. This formatter follows that rule, so “The Lord of the Rings” stays correct, and “A Tale of Two Cities” keeps its leading A.

## Tips

A few things worth knowing before you rely on the result — most of them are about the numbers you put in, rather than the tool itself:

- For headings, Title Case is the safe choice; for body text, use Sentence case.
- Check proper nouns after formatting — a formatter cannot know that 'iPhone' needs a lowercase i.
- Use the Word Counter for a fuller breakdown of the same text.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is Title Case?

Capitalising the first letter of every major word in a title, while leaving small words (a, an, the, and, of, in) lowercase unless they start or end the title. For example: 'The Quick Brown Fox Jumps Over the Lazy Dog'. Try it with your own numbers in the [Text Formatter](/text-formatter) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### What is the difference between Title Case and Capitalise Each Word?

Title Case leaves small words lowercase in the middle of a title; Capitalise Each Word capitalises every word without exception. Use Title Case for published headings and Capitalise Each Word for labels and lists. Try it with your own numbers in the [Text Formatter](/text-formatter) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### Does Sentence case change proper nouns?

It lowercases everything except the first letter of each sentence, so a name like 'London' would become 'london'. Check proper nouns after formatting and fix them by hand. Try it with your own numbers in the [Text Formatter](/text-formatter) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### What do I need to use the Text Formatter?

Just Text to format and Format. Enter those values and the result appears straight away — no account or download needed. If you are unsure about a value, try a rough figure first and then refine it — the result updates instantly.
